Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette:
Dorothy is a 78-year-old graphic designer who has been married for fifty-two years. She sought help seven months after a wildfire destroyed her home and the neighborhood she had lived in for four decades. She and her husband had been given a mandatory evacuation order with only minutes to gather their belongings. As they drove away, the smoke was so thick she could barely see the road, and the roar of the fire was deafening. She remembers the smell of burning pine and the sound of trees exploding. What she cannot forget is the moment she realized her elderly neighbor, a widow named Helen, had not made it out. Dorothy had knocked on Helen's door, but Helen had refused to leave, saying she would rather die in her own home. Dorothy still hears that door slamming shut as she turned away. Helen's body was found in the rubble three days later.

In the months since the fire, Dorothy has not been able to return to her work as a graphic designer. Her home was rebuilt, but she cannot bear to be there alone. She spends most of her days at her daughter's house, where she has taken over the cleaning. She scrubs the kitchen counters repeatedly, reorganizes the pantry by color and size, and vacuums the same hallway three times a day. She tells herself that if everything is in order, nothing bad can happen. When her daughter's partner comes home from work and the front door slams, Dorothy's heart seizes. She freezes, her hands gripping whatever object is nearest, and she is certain that something terrible is about to happen. The world, she has come to believe, is a dangerous place where catastrophe can strike without warning. What happened to her was deeply unfair, and nothing has been done about it-no one was held accountable for the inadequate evacuation warning, and Helen's death was written off as a tragic choice. These thoughts crowd her mind every time she hears that door, and she finds herself scrubbing the countertops even harder, as if she can erase the injustice by making her surroundings spotless.

Dorothy has also developed a habit of dwelling on how the fire could have been prevented. She replays the day in her mind, wondering if she had called the authorities earlier, if she had insisted Helen leave, if she had grabbed the fire extinguisher instead of the photo albums. This rumination does not bring relief; it only makes the memory feel more vivid, more present. Sometimes, when she is washing dishes, the smell of rubbing alcohol from a first-aid kit in the bathroom wafts into the kitchen, and she is instantly back in the smoke, the heat on her face, the roar in her ears. The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over. At other times, she can recall what happened but feels completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. The event was so extreme that she sometimes finds it hard to believe it actually happened to her. She has tried to push the memory out of her mind entirely, but the harder she tries to erase it, the more it intrudes, especially when she is cleaning or when a door slams.

Her avoidance has taken a toll on her marriage. She refuses to go to the grocery store because the wine aisle smells of alcohol, and she has stopped attending her weekly bridge club because someone there lost a son to cancer and the talk of losing loved ones is unbearable. She now believes that loss is everywhere, waiting for her. Her husband has grown frustrated, and they have not had a conversation that lasted more than five minutes in weeks. She knows she is driving him away, but she cannot stop. The cleaning, the rumination, the attempts to erase the memory-these are the only things that make her feel even a little bit safe. What finally brought her to therapy was her daughter's ultimatum: either get help or move out. Dorothy is afraid that if she stops cleaning, the world will fall apart again. But she is also afraid of losing her family. She does not know how to live in a world that feels so dangerous, and she is hoping, quietly, that someone can tell her how.
